overview:
In the context of the Jain AI ontology v1.0, “search aliases” are alternative labels, names, or phrasings attached to a single underlying concept node so that users can successfully find that concept even when they do not know, or do not use, its canonical label. The ontology contains 52 domains and 1676 core topic nodes, each of which may be known by different terms across Jain traditions (Digambara, Śvetāmbara, Sthānakavāsī, Terāpanth), languages (Prakrit, Sanskrit, Hindi, Gujarati, English, etc.), and pedagogical contexts (youth education, lay practice, technical philosophy). Search aliases are the structured way the system captures this diversity of naming while preserving a single, stable conceptual identity for each topic.

From an information-architecture perspective, a search alias is not a separate node in the ontology but a string (or set of strings) associated with a node to support retrieval, navigation, and user-friendly discovery. For example, a single topic node on “anekāntavāda” may carry aliases such as “anekantvad”, “doctrine of non-one-sidedness”, “non-absolutism”, or common transliteration variants like “anekantavada”. When a user searches with any of these forms, the retrieval engine maps the query to the same underlying topic node. This design follows broader ontology practice, where synonyms and aliases are used to bridge between technical labels and the varied language of real users, while keeping the ontology’s conceptual structure coherent and non-duplicated.

Within the Jain AI system, search aliases are especially important because Jain terminology has evolved over centuries, and different communities may prefer distinct labels for the same doctrinal or historical idea. A term like “karma” may appear as “kamma” in Prakrit, “karmā” in Sanskrit, and have modern explanatory phrases such as “subtle matter that binds the soul”. Similarly, canonical text names, sectarian designations, and practice-related terms often have multiple spellings and colloquial forms. Search aliases allow the ontology to respect this plurality without fragmenting the knowledge graph: the canonical label is chosen according to the architecture rules (e.g., tradition-aware, text-grounded naming), while aliases record the other legitimate ways that users might refer to the same node.

Technically, search aliases are part of the retrieval and ranking pipeline. When a user issues a query, the system expands the query using known aliases, normalizes transliteration and spelling variants, and then matches against the ontology’s labels and alias fields. This improves recall (the system finds more relevant nodes) without sacrificing precision (results still correspond to well-defined topics). The architecture also allows different guide modes—such as Foundations Guide, Primary Text Guide, Digambara Study Guide, or Youth and Family Guide—to prioritize different aliases in display. For instance, a youth-oriented guide might surface simpler English aliases, while a Primary Text Guide emphasizes canonical Prakrit or Sanskrit labels.

Because the system is source-grounded, search aliases are not invented freely; they are curated from corpus tiers (A–D) and, where possible, tied to attested usage in primary texts, traditional commentaries, and responsible community education. Aliases derived from lower-confidence materials (tiers E–F) are quarantined or marked as experimental and are not treated as authoritative labels. This ensures that the convenience of flexible search does not erode the doctrinal and philological integrity of the ontology. In addition, the architecture rules require that material claims be mapped to sources and that disagreements or uncertainties be surfaced. For aliases, this means that if different traditions use conflicting labels for a concept, the ontology records these differences explicitly rather than collapsing them into a single, misleading name.

Finally, search aliases play a role in user safety and authority boundaries. The system must not present itself as a Maharaj Saheb, Acharya, monk, nun, or guru, and it must escalate queries involving fasting, self-harm, medical or legal decisions, or dikṣā. Aliases for sensitive topics—such as “sallekhanā”, “santhārā”, or extreme fasting practices—are carefully managed so that searches still reach accurate, source-grounded information, but the responses remain within the non-prescriptive, advisory scope defined by the architecture. In this way, search aliases serve both usability and ethical responsibility: they help users find what they are looking for, while the underlying ontology and guide modes ensure that what is found is contextualized, properly sourced, and framed within appropriate boundaries of authority and care.

primary_sources.title: Jain AI Ontology Architecture v1.0 (Source-Grounded Jain Study Guides and Advice System)
primary_sources.author: Jain AI Project Team
primary_sources.translation: This architecture document defines the authority boundaries, guide modes, answer pipeline, mandatory escalation rules, corpus tiers, and ontology structure (52 domains and 1676 core topic nodes) for the Jain AI system. It implicitly specifies the need for search aliases by emphasizing tradition-aware retrieval, multiple guide modes, and careful mapping of material claims to sources.
primary_sources.notes: Although not a classical Jain scripture, this document is a primary design text for the Jain AI ontology. It establishes the conceptual framework within which search aliases operate: aliases must respect authority boundaries, be grounded in verified textual and community sources, and support different guide modes without collapsing doctrinal distinctions. The mention of ontology v1.0 with 52 domains and 1676 topic nodes provides the structural context in which aliases are attached to nodes rather than treated as independent concepts.

misconceptions.myth: Search aliases are separate doctrinal concepts or independent ontology nodes.
misconceptions.reality: In the Jain AI ontology, search aliases are alternative labels attached to a single underlying topic node. They do not create new concepts; they simply record different ways users may refer to the same, well-defined idea, preserving conceptual coherence while improving search and navigation.

misconceptions.myth: Any commonly used phrase or spelling can be added as a search alias without reference to sources.
misconceptions.reality: Aliases are curated and, where possible, grounded in attested usage from primary texts, traditional commentaries, and responsible community education. The architecture’s corpus tiers (A–D vs. E–F) and source-mapping requirements mean that aliases are not freely invented; low-confidence or speculative forms are quarantined or clearly marked to avoid misleading users.

misconceptions.myth: Search aliases are purely technical and have no impact on how different Jain traditions are represented.
misconceptions.reality: Aliases are deeply tradition-aware. Different sects and communities may use distinct labels for the same or closely related ideas, and the ontology records these differences explicitly. Guide modes (e.g., Digambara Study Guide, Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka Study Guide, Youth and Family Guide) can prioritize different aliases in display, ensuring that users see terminology appropriate to their context while still being linked to a shared, well-structured conceptual graph.

misconceptions.myth: Once a search alias is defined, it can safely replace the canonical label in all user interfaces.
misconceptions.reality: The architecture distinguishes between canonical labels and aliases. Canonical labels are chosen according to text-grounded and tradition-aware criteria, while aliases support retrieval and user-friendly phrasing. Some interfaces may surface aliases for accessibility, but the canonical label remains the primary reference point for doctrinal, historical, and philological precision, especially in technical or academic modes.
